content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published updated guidelines in July 2018 for the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These guidelines were developed based on evidence, including surveys conducted to assess the acceptability, feasibility, and preferences related to the recommendations. The surveys targeted three groups: individuals living with HCV infection, healthcare workers (HCWs) providing care to these individuals, and national program managers. Surveys Conducted Three online surveys were designed using the SurveyMonkey® tool and were made available in English and French. These surveys were piloted and adjusted as necessary. The surveys targeted the following groups: 1. People living with HCV infection: Key civil society networks and guideline development group members were contacted, and snowball sampling was encouraged. 2. Healthcare workers (HCWs): Networks providing care to individuals with HCV infection and guideline development group members were approached to disseminate the survey. 3. Program managers: National program managers were contacted through WHO regional offices and advisors to distribute the survey within their regions. Survey Results Survey 1: People Living with HCV Infection Among 112 respondents, 70% were male, and over 80% were aged between 30 and 60 years. Respondents represented all WHO regions except the Eastern Mediterranean, with fewer participants from the African and European regions. 87% of respondents reported receiving antiviral treatment, while 13% were aware of their HCV infection but had not yet been treated. Of those treated, 65% received care in hospital settings, and 25% in private clinics. When asked about a treat all policy (treating all HCV patients with antiviral drugs regardless of disease stage), 20% reported that their clinic already had such a policy, and 30% expressed no concerns. However, some respondents raised concerns about drug-drug interactions, long-term side effects, treatment acceptability, and costs. Survey 2: Healthcare Workers A total of 145 HCWs from 27 countries responded, representing all WHO regions. Their roles included hospital physicians, primary care physicians, private clinic physicians, nurses, pharmacists, community health workers, and others. 50% of HCWs reported that their workplace already had a treat all policy. The most commonly perceived challenges were capacity limitations to meet demand (30%), difficulties in identifying eligible patients, lack of HCW skills, and issues with patient adherence and retention in care. Survey 3: Program Managers Ten program managers from countries including Brazil, Cameroon, Colombia, Egypt, Georgia, Iceland, Morocco, Pakistan, South Africa, and Zimbabwe responded. All reported having viral hepatitis strategies and action plans in place. Three countries had programs treating people in prisons, and one had special clinics for people who inject drugs. 50% of program managers reported having a treat all policy in their country. Challenges included a lack of testing strategies, insufficient funding, lack of HCW skills, and difficulties in identifying eligible patients. Key Findings A treat all policy was widely perceived as feasible and desirable by individuals living with HCV infection, HCWs, and program managers. The most common concerns among individuals with HCV infection were potential drug-drug interactions, long-term side effects, treatment acceptability, and costs. For HCWs, the greatest challenges were capacity limitations, identifying eligible patients, and costs. Program managers identified the lack of a testing strategy and insufficient funding as the most significant barriers to implementing a treat all policy.
